reason: The sources provide multi-site corroboration for the discovery, scale, immense luminosity, and star clusters of the Tarantula Nebula.
story: In 1751, French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille surveyed the southern skies from the Cape of Good Hope and spotted a hazy patch in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Named the Tarantula Nebula for its sprawling, spider-like tendrils of gas, this cosmic nursery lies roughly 160,000 light-years away in the constellation Dorado. Despite that staggering distance, it shines brightly enough to be seen with the naked eye. The nebula is the most luminous and violent star-forming region in the entire Local Group of galaxies, powered at its heart by the dense star cluster R136, home to some of the most massive stars ever discovered. Its energy output is almost incomprehensible: if the Tarantula Nebula were placed at the distance of our familiar Orion Nebula, it would cover forty percent of the night sky and shine so brilliantly that it would cast visible shadows on the ground.
angle: If the Tarantula Nebula sat as close to Earth as the Orion Nebula, its light would cast visible shadows on the ground at night.

claims.claim: The Tarantula Nebula is also known by the astronomical designation 30 Doradus.
The Tarantula Nebula is located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
The nebula is located in the constellation Dorado.
French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first cataloged the nebula during an expedition in 1751.
Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille observed the nebula from the Cape of Good Hope.
Lacaille cataloged the object as a nebula of the first class because no stars were visible through his telescope.
German astronomer Johann Bode included 30 Doradus in his 1801 star atlas Uranographia.
The name Tarantula Nebula arose because its glowing gas filaments and dusty tendrils resemble the legs of a tarantula.
The Tarantula Nebula is situated roughly 160,000 light-years away from Earth.
The Tarantula Nebula is the largest and most energetic star-forming region in the Local Group of galaxies.
If the Tarantula Nebula were placed at the distance of the Orion Nebula, it would cast visible shadows on Earth.
The Tarantula Nebula spans roughly 1,000 light-years in diameter.
The nebula can be seen from Earth with the naked eye despite being outside the Milky Way galaxy.
At the core of the nebula lies the dense, compact star cluster R136.
Cluster R136 produces most of the radiation and energy that powers the nebula's glow.
R136 contains some of the most massive and luminous stars known in the universe.
Astronomers previously debated whether the heart of R136 was a cluster of stars or a single supermassive star weighing roughly 1,000 solar masses.
The Tarantula Nebula contains the older star cluster Hodge 301, where dozens of stars have exploded as supernovae.
Supernova 1987A occurred on the outskirts of the Tarantula Nebula.
Supernova 1987A was the closest observed supernova since the invention of the telescope.

disputed: Position within the Large Magellanic Cloud: S1 places the nebula in the south-east corner, whereas S4 describes it as near the northeastern edge. A script should simply state it is located in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Distance estimates: Sources report slightly differing distances, ranging from about 160,000 light-years (S1, S4), 161,000 light-years (S2), over 160,000 light-years (S3), to around 170,000 light-years (S5). A script should say roughly 160,000 light-years.

Physical diameter: S3, S4, and S6 describe the nebula as spanning roughly or more than 1,000 light-years, while S1 cites an estimated diameter range of 200 to 570 parsecs (650 to 1,860 light-years). A script should attribute it as roughly 1,000 light-years across.
